processing: Ripe elderberries are dried, with stems and leaves removed, then boiled and strained. Heat matters here: raw unripe berries, stems and leaves contain sambunigrin, which cooking eliminates.
harvest_season: Not tied to a prized picking in the sources; bought dried year round.
appearance_liquor: Deep purple-red and opaque when simmered strongly.
appearance_wet: Plump, soft, dark berries that are strained out.
taste_profile: Sweet and tart with an earthy undertone, often paired with cinnamon, ginger, orange or honey.

brewing.notes: Simmer 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried berries per cup for about 15 minutes, then strain. Never use raw berries, stems or leaves.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage, as whole dried berries or in bags. As with other dried fruit, the fresher pack keeps more colour and flavour, so check the packing date and look for clean berries with no stems.
description:
Elderberry tea is an infusion of the dark berries of the elder, a hedgerow plant familiar in Britain. It is a fruit drink, with no tea leaf in it.

The important thing is the heat. Raw unripe berries, along with stems and leaves, contain sambunigrin, which degrades to hydrogen cyanide and can cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Cooking takes care of it, which is why simmering is the standard method and why dried berries should come free of stems.

The cup is sweet-tart and earthy. Recipes differ on simmering time, so adjust to taste. Cinnamon, ginger, orange or honey all suit it.

In any blend, read the ingredients to see how much elderberry it really holds.
history: Little is documented specifically about elderberry tea as a named drink, and there is no reliable date or person to attach to it. Today it is mostly a home recipe and a wellness-shop product.
